result:
The first time I saw the ocean, I was six years old. My family had driven for hours to reach the coast, and when we finally stepped onto the warm sand, the vast blue stretched endlessly before me. I remember crouching down, letting the water lap at my toes, and feeling something shift inside—like the world had suddenly become both smaller and infinitely larger. That moment taught me that wonder isn’t just in grand gestures but in the quiet, unassuming things: the way sunlight dances on water, the salt in the air, the way the horizon blurs where earth meets sky.

Years later, I still chase those moments of quiet awe. Sometimes it’s in a crowded city, watching a stranger’s laughter light up their face. Other times, it’s in the stillness of early morning, when the world feels like it’s holding its breath. I’ve learned that beauty isn’t always loud or obvious—it’s in the way a streetlamp glows against the snow, or how a single dandelion pushes through a crack in the pavement. It’s in the stories people tell, in the way a book can make you feel less alone, in the quiet resilience of nature pushing through concrete.

I think we spend so much time rushing that we forget to pause. To really *see*. The ocean taught me that. It’s a reminder that life isn’t just about the destination but the way the light hits the waves at dawn, the way the tide pulls back and leaves treasures behind. Maybe that’s why I write—to capture those fleeting, shimmering moments before they slip away. Because some things are too precious to let vanish without a trace.
